title: Contract Modifications Under ASC 606
learning_objectives: Identify the four types of contract modification accounting
Apply the decision framework to determine modification treatment
Calculate revenue adjustments for each modification type
Prepare journal entries for contract modifications
Understand the impact of modifications on performance obligations and transaction price

common_question_types: Multiple choice identifying correct modification treatment
Task-based simulations requiring modification analysis and journal entries

introduction.definition: A contract modification is a change in the scope or price (or both) of a contract that is approved by the parties to the contract. A modification may be approved in writing, by oral agreement, or implied by customary business practices.
key_concepts: Modification must be approved by parties - unilateral actions don't qualify
Can involve changes to scope (what is being delivered) or price (how much is being paid) or both
Approval can be formal (written amendment) or informal (oral agreement, implied by conduct)
Accounting treatment depends on specific facts and circumstances
introduction.importance: Contract modifications are common in business, especially in long-term contracts. Proper accounting is critical because different treatments result in different timing and amounts of revenue recognition.
common_scenarios: Customer requests additional goods or services beyond original contract
Parties agree to change specifications or scope of work
Price adjustments due to changed circumstances
Exercise of options included in original contract (may or may not be modification)
Renewals or extensions of service contracts

is_it_a_modification.key_question: Has the scope or price of the contract changed?

required_elements.description: There must be a change to what is being provided (scope) or what is being paid (price) or both
Both customer and entity must approve the change - unilateral actions are not modifications

not_a_modification.scenario: Exercise of option included in original contract at price specified in original contract
not_a_modification.explanation: This is part of original contract, not a modification. Evaluate whether option represents a material right.
not_a_modification.example: Software contract grants customer option to add 100 users at $50/user. Customer exercises option. This is not a modification; it's fulfillment of original contract terms.

not_a_modification.scenario: Variability contemplated in original contract is resolved
not_a_modification.explanation: If original contract included variable consideration and that variability is resolved, it's an update to transaction price, not a modification.
not_a_modification.example: Construction contract includes performance bonus if completed by certain date. Completion occurs - bonus earned. This updates transaction price under original contract.

not_a_modification.explanation: If entity decides to reduce price without customer agreement, this is a change in transaction price (variable consideration), not a modification.
not_a_modification.example: Entity decides to waive late fees to maintain customer relationship. Customer doesn't formally agree. Update transaction price; not a modification.

forms_of_approval: Oral agreement (may be evidenced by emails, notes, partial performance)
Implied by customary business practices (e.g., entity always accepts certain change requests)

timing_of_approval.principle: Account for modification when approved, even if parties haven't agreed on price
timing_of_approval.exception: If scope is approved but price not yet determined, assess whether it's possible to estimate price. If yes, account for modification. If no, wait until price is determinable.
timing_of_approval.example: Construction change order approved for additional work. Price to be negotiated. If entity can reasonably estimate the price, account for modification immediately. Otherwise, wait.

four_modification_treatments.overview: ASC 606 provides four potential accounting treatments for contract modifications. The appropriate treatment depends on the specific facts and circumstances of the modification.

step_1.question: Does the modification add distinct goods or services priced at their standalone selling price (SSP)?

step_2.question: Are the remaining goods or services distinct from those already transferred?
step_2.if_yes: Treatment #2: PROSPECTIVE (terminate old contract, create new contract for remaining POs)

step_3.question: Are the remaining goods or services distinct or not distinct?
step_3.answer: Since we reached Step 3, they are NOT distinct (failed Step 2)
step_3.result: Treatment #3: CUMULATIVE CATCH-UP (adjust as if modification was part of original contract)
step_3.note: If modification includes mix of distinct and non-distinct goods/services, use Treatment #4: COMBINATION

treatment_1_separate_contract.title: Treatment #1: Account for as Separate Contract
treatment_1_separate_contract.when_to_use: Use when ALL of the following criteria are met:
criteria: The modification adds distinct goods or services to the contract
The price for the additional goods or services reflects their standalone selling price (SSP)
treatment_1_separate_contract.both_required: Both criteria must be met. If only one is met, this treatment does not apply.

accounting_treatment.description: Account for the modification as a separate, new contract. The original contract continues unchanged.
accounting_treatment.impact_on_original_contract: None - continue recognizing revenue on original contract as if modification never occurred
accounting_treatment.impact_on_modified_contract: Recognize revenue on additional goods/services as a separate contract using five-step model

facts: Original contract (Jan 1, Year 1): 500 user licenses for $500,000 (annual subscription)
Entity's SSP: $1,000 per user license per year
Modification (June 1, Year 1): Customer adds 100 user licenses
Modification price: $50,000 for remaining 7 months of Year 1 ($100,000 annualized)
Analysis: 100 licenses are distinct (sold separately regularly). Price of $100,000 annual is at SSP ($1,000/user).

analysis.criterion_1_distinct: YES - User licenses are distinct. Entity sells them separately regularly.
analysis.criterion_2_ssp: YES - $100,000 annual price equals SSP (100 users × $1,000/user)

accounting: Original contract: Continue recognizing $500,000 ratably over Year 1 (already recognized $250,000 through May 31)
Separate new contract: Recognize $50,000 ratably from June 1 through Dec 31 (7 months)

journal_entries.entry:
DR Cash $50,000
   CR Contract Liability - New Contract $50,000

journal_entries.date: June 30, Year 1 (monthly recognition for new contract)
journal_entries.entry:
DR Contract Liability - New Contract $7,143
   CR Revenue $7,143
journal_entries.description: Recognize 1 month of new contract ($50,000 / 7 months)

cpa_exam_tips: Look for words like 'at market price,' 'at SSP,' 'at normal rates' - suggests criterion 2 met
If problem states entity regularly sells items separately, criterion 1 likely met
Separate contract treatment is simplest - original contract unaffected
This treatment is exception; most modifications don't qualify

treatment_2_prospective.title: Treatment #2: Prospective Treatment (Terminate Old, Create New)
criteria: Modification does NOT qualify as separate contract (failed Treatment #1)
AND remaining goods or services ARE distinct from those already transferred

accounting_treatment.description: Terminate the old contract and create a new contract for the remaining performance obligations.
steps: Calculate new transaction price: Original remaining balance + Modification consideration
Calculate new obligations: Original remaining goods/services + Modification additions
Allocate new transaction price to new obligations
Recognize revenue prospectively using new amounts
Do NOT adjust revenue previously recognized

formula.new_transaction_price: Original Transaction Price - Revenue Recognized to Date + Modification Consideration
formula.description: This becomes the transaction price for the 'new contract' going forward

facts: Original contract (Jan 1, Year 1): 1,000 hours of consulting at $300/hour = $300,000
Through June 30, Year 1: 400 hours delivered, $120,000 revenue recognized
Remaining: 600 hours, $180,000 remaining revenue
Modification (July 1, Year 1): Add 500 hours of distinct consulting services
Modification price: $120,000 (discounted from $150,000 SSP)
Analysis: Additional hours are distinct but NOT at SSP (discounted)

analysis.criterion_1_distinct: YES - Consulting hours are distinct from each other
analysis.criterion_2_ssp: NO - $120,000 is less than $150,000 SSP (20% discount)
analysis.conclusion: Does NOT qualify as separate contract
analysis.remaining_distinct: YES - Remaining 600 hours are distinct from 400 hours already delivered

accounting_calculation: New rate per hour: $300,000 / 1,100 hours = $272.73 per hour
Going forward: Recognize $272.73 per hour (vs. original $300/hour)

journal_entries.entry:
DR Accounts Receivable $120,000
   CR Contract Liability - Modified Contract $120,000

DR Contract Asset or Contract Liability $XXX
   CR Revenue $XXX

cpa_exam_tips: Prospective = no adjustment to past revenue
Calculate new combined price and new combined work to get new rate/allocation
Remaining services must be distinct from those already provided
This treatment is common for time-and-materials or unit-based contracts

treatment_3_cumulative_catchup.title: Treatment #3: Cumulative Catch-Up Adjustment
criteria: Modification does NOT qualify as separate contract (failed Treatment #1)
AND remaining goods or services are NOT distinct from those already transferred

accounting_treatment.description: Account for the modification as if it had been part of the original contract from inception. Recognize a cumulative catch-up adjustment in the period of modification.
steps: Calculate modified total transaction price: Original price + Modification consideration
Calculate modified total performance obligation: Original scope + Modification additions
Determine percentage complete based on modified total
Calculate cumulative revenue that should have been recognized: Modified total × Percentage complete
Compare to revenue actually recognized to date
Recognize catch-up adjustment in current period for difference

formula.modified_total_costs: Original Estimated Costs + Modification Additional Costs (if using cost-to-cost)
formula.percentage_complete: Costs Incurred to Date / Modified Total Costs
formula.catchup_adjustment: Cumulative Revenue Should Have Recognized - Revenue Already Recognized

facts: Original contract (Jan 1, Year 1): Build office building for $10,000,000
Original estimated costs: $8,000,000
Through June 30, Year 1: Costs incurred $3,200,000 (40% complete)
Revenue recognized through June 30: $4,000,000 (40% × $10M)
Modification (July 1, Year 1): Add another floor to building
Modification price: $1,500,000
Modification estimated costs: $1,200,000
Analysis: Additional floor is NOT distinct from original building - highly integrated

analysis.criterion_1_distinct: NO - Additional floor is part of integrated building
analysis.remaining_distinct: NO - Remaining construction not distinct from work already completed

accounting_calculation: Costs incurred to date: $3,200,000 (no change - modification work hasn't started)
Explanation: Percentage complete decreased from 40% to 34.78% because total project is now larger. This creates small catch-up reduction.

alternative_example_with_positive_adjust.scenario: Same facts, but modification price is $2,000,000 instead of $1,500,000
calculation: Explanation: Higher modification price more than offsets dilution from larger project scope.

journal_entries.date: July 1, Year 1 (using alternative example with positive adjustment)
journal_entries.entry:
DR Accounts Receivable $2,000,000
   CR Contract Liability $2,000,000

DR Contract Asset $173,600
   CR Revenue (Catch-Up Adjustment) $173,600

going_forward: Future revenue will be based on modified total transaction price of $12,000,000
Future percentage complete calculations use modified total costs of $9,200,000
Example: At Dec 31 Year 1, if costs incurred are $5,000,000 total:

cpa_exam_tips: Cumulative catch-up = adjust as if modification was in original contract
This treatment is common for construction, development, and other integrated projects
Catch-up adjustment can be positive (more revenue) or negative (less revenue)
Negative catch-up occurs when percentage complete decreases due to expanded scope
Always show the revised percentage complete calculation - often tested!

treatment_4_combination.title: Treatment #4: Combination Approach
criteria: Some remaining goods or services that ARE distinct from those already transferred
AND some remaining goods or services that are NOT distinct from those already transferred

approach: For distinct remaining goods/services: Apply prospective treatment (Treatment #2)
For non-distinct remaining goods/services: Apply cumulative catch-up treatment (Treatment #3)

facts: Original contract: (1) Construct facility for $8,000,000, (2) Provide training for $500,000. Total: $8,500,000
Through modification date: Construction 50% complete ($4,000,000 recognized), Training not started
Modification: Add additional features to facility (not distinct from existing construction) for $1,200,000, Add additional training modules (distinct from original training) for $300,000

analysis.construction_modification: NOT distinct from original construction - integrated into facility
analysis.training_modification: Distinct from original training - separate modules

cpa_exam_tips: Combination approach is less commonly tested but can appear in complex simulations
Separately analyze each performance obligation to determine distinct vs. not distinct
Apply appropriate treatment to each category
Show your work clearly - partial credit often available

unapproved_change_orders.scenario: Entity has performed work pursuant to a change order that has not yet been approved by customer

accounting.general_rule: Do not account for as a modification until approved
exception_criteria: It is highly probable that customer will approve the change order and price, AND
The amount can be reasonably estimated
accounting.note: Apply constraint on variable consideration - may need to recognize at lower amount than claimed if significant reversal risk exists

unapproved_change_orders.example: Construction contractor performs extra work costing $100,000, will claim $150,000. Customer hasn't approved but has acknowledged work was needed. If highly probable customer will pay, may recognize revenue (possibly constrained amount below $150,000). Otherwise, wait for approval.

contract_renewals_and_extensions.question: Are renewals and extensions contract modifications?

if_optional_renewal_in_original_contract.treatment: Not a modification - part of original contract
if_optional_renewal_in_original_contract.consideration: Evaluate whether renewal option provided customer with material right
if_optional_renewal_in_original_contract.example: Annual software subscription with renewal option at same price. Renewal is not modification; evaluate if renewal option was material right in original contract.

if_renewal_negotiated_after_original_con.rationale: Original contract has ended; new contract begins
if_renewal_negotiated_after_original_con.example: Software subscription ends Dec 31 Year 1. Customer signs new subscription starting Jan 1 Year 2. This is new contract, not modification.

if_extension_agreed_before_original_cont.apply_framework: Use decision framework to determine appropriate treatment
if_extension_agreed_before_original_cont.example: Consulting contract for Year 1 is extended to cover Year 2, agreed in November Year 1. This is modification; apply four-treatment framework.

price_changes_without_scope_changes.scenario: Parties agree to change price but scope of work remains the same
price_changes_without_scope_changes.is_it_a_modification: YES - modification can be change in price, scope, or both
price_changes_without_scope_changes.analysis: Since no additional goods/services added, cannot be separate contract. Apply prospective or cumulative catch-up depending on whether remaining services are distinct.
price_changes_without_scope_changes.example: Consulting contract for 1,000 hours at $200/hour = $200,000. After 400 hours delivered, parties agree to reduce price to $150,000 for entire contract (to preserve relationship). This is modification. Remaining 600 hours are distinct from delivered 400 hours, so use prospective treatment: New price for remaining work = $150,000 - $80,000 already recognized = $70,000 for remaining 600 hours = $116.67/hour going forward.

decision_tree.title: Contract Modification Decision Tree
decision_tree.description: Step-by-step process to determine accounting treatment

steps.question: Is there a change in scope or price approved by both parties?
steps.if_no: Not a modification. May be update to variable consideration or other transaction price adjustment.
steps.if_yes: It is a modification. Proceed to next step.

steps.question: Does the modification add distinct goods/services AT their standalone selling price?
steps.test: Both criteria must be met: (1) Goods/services are distinct, AND (2) Price equals SSP
steps.if_yes: Treatment #1: SEPARATE CONTRACT. Account for as new contract; original contract unaffected.

steps.question: Are the remaining goods/services distinct from those already transferred?
steps.test: Evaluate whether remaining items are distinct (both capable and in context) from already delivered items
steps.if_yes: Treatment #2: PROSPECTIVE. Terminate old contract, create new contract for remaining POs. New price = remaining balance + modification consideration.

steps.question: Are remaining goods/services distinct or not distinct? (Or mix of both?)
steps.answer_not_distinct: Treatment #3: CUMULATIVE CATCH-UP. Adjust as if modification was in original contract. Recognize catch-up adjustment.
steps.answer_mix: Treatment #4: COMBINATION. Apply prospective treatment to distinct portions and cumulative catch-up to non-distinct portions.

treatments.impact_on_modification: Account for as separate new contract
treatments.example: Add user licenses at standard price

treatments.impact_on_modification: Create new contract for remaining + modification
treatments.example: Add consulting hours to time-and-materials contract

treatments.when_to_use: Remaining services NOT distinct from delivered
treatments.impact_on_original: Adjust as if modification was in original
treatments.example: Add floor to building under construction

treatments.when_to_use: Mix of distinct and non-distinct remaining services
treatments.example: Add features to building (non-distinct) and training (distinct)

information_needed: Standalone selling prices of modified goods/services

process: Test for separate contract treatment (distinct + at SSP?)
If not separate, test whether remaining services distinct from delivered

calculations: For separate contract: Calculate revenue on new contract separately
For prospective: Calculate new transaction price for remaining work
For cumulative catch-up: Calculate modified total, percentage complete, catch-up adjustment

ongoing: Use modified amounts for future revenue recognition

multiple_choice_tips: Identify modification treatment questions quickly - look for words like 'amended,' 'changed scope,' 'added services'
First test: Is it at SSP? If yes and distinct, it's separate contract - easiest answer
Second test: Are remaining services distinct from delivered? Often the key question
Cumulative catch-up is for integrated projects where modification can't be separated
If problem describes construction project with scope increase, think cumulative catch-up
If problem describes service contract with additional distinct services, think prospective or separate contract
simulation_strategies: Read facts carefully to understand what was in original contract vs. modification
Create a timeline showing original contract, performance to date, and modification
Work through decision framework systematically - show your analysis
For cumulative catch-up problems, clearly show modified total and percentage complete calculation
For prospective problems, clearly show new combined transaction price for remaining work
Prepare supporting schedules before journal entries
Label catch-up adjustments clearly in journal entries
common_mistakes_to_avoid: Assuming all modifications are separate contracts - this is rare!
Forgetting to test BOTH criteria for separate contract (distinct AND at SSP)
Confusing prospective and cumulative catch-up - focus on whether remaining services are distinct
In cumulative catch-up, using old percentage complete instead of recalculating based on modified total
Forgetting that prospective treatment means NO adjustment to past revenue
Not clearly showing which treatment you're applying - state it explicitly
time_management: Don't overcomplicate - work through decision framework methodically
If treatment is separate contract, remaining work is simple - don't overthink
Cumulative catch-up calculations take most time - allocate accordingly
Show calculations even if not required - helps you think clearly and earns partial credit

key_takeaways: Contract modification = change in scope or price approved by both parties
Four possible accounting treatments depending on specific facts
Separate contract treatment requires distinct goods/services at SSP (both criteria)
Prospective treatment applies when remaining services distinct from delivered services
Cumulative catch-up applies when remaining services NOT distinct from delivered services
Combination approach used when mix of distinct and non-distinct remaining services
Work through decision framework systematically - don't skip steps
Cumulative catch-up requires recalculating percentage complete based on modified totals
Prospective treatment never adjusts past revenue - only affects future recognition

memorization_aids.decision_framework: Separate (distinct + SSP) → Prospective (remaining distinct) → Catch-up (remaining not distinct)
memorization_aids.prospective_vs_catchup: Prospective = distinct remaining (no past adjustment), Catch-up = integrated remaining (adjust past)
